messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] could I make some members of mcmc::chains protected?
parts:
DEPDENCIES: No, we can't have Rcpp dependencies
in anything in Stan. Do NOT, under any circumstances,
link anything in Stan proper into anything depending
on R. For one, it destroys modularity. For two, it
breaks our license because of the copyleft in R.

You can extend the class and put it in the R package.
You can write wrappers to convert. But you can't
have our basic data structures depend in any way on R.

PRIVACY: The usual thinking is to keep the private
bits of a class private (and ideally final). Not protected,
which isn't very strong in C++. The goal is to make
classes which are guaranteed to be in proper states.
As soon as you unprivatize the data, all bets are
off and reasoning about programs gets much harder.

Having said that, our API is hardly safely laid
out. I was much better about this in Java.

And C++ is inherently unsafe by allowing you raw
memory access.

- Bob

I guess I did not make myself understood. 

If I have _samples be protected.  I could inherit mcmc::chains in 
RStan package, in which I have to use Rcpp and R's stuff.  That is, in *RStan*
I would have:

class chains_for_R : public stan::mcmc {
public:
   SEXP get_samples_for_R (size_t j, ....) {
   }
   ....
}

This definitely would not change Stan's dependencies at all and it keeps 
the molecularity.  However, if _samples is private, I could not use it 
directly in the derived class so that I could extend. 

To balance PRIVACY and extendability, I think sometimes we need protected.
--
Jiqiang

parts:
Addressing Matt's concerns, I'd rather make things
private and then when we realize we need to make
them protected, make them protected. Protected
variables complicate interfaces (requiring more doc
and testing in the ideal case) and lower protections
on state.

Answers to Jiqiang below inline.

On 5/30/12 12:47 PM, Jiqiang Guo wrote:
> I guess I did not make myself understood.

It's tough in e-mail about code, but I get it now.
See below.

> If I have _samples be protected. I could inherit mcmc::chains in
> RStan package, in which I have to use Rcpp and R's stuff. That is, in
> *RStan*
> I would have:
>
> class chains_for_R : public stan::mcmc {
> public:
> SEXP get_samples_for_R (size_t j, ....) {
> }
> ....
> }

I was thinking you'd just hold a reference to
an mcmc::chains object and then wrap the results.

> This definitely would not change Stan's dependencies at all and it keeps
> the molecularity. However, if _samples is private, I could not use it
> directly in the derived class so that I could extend.
>
> To balance PRIVACY and extendability, I think sometimes we need protected.

That's what protected is there for!

The reason protected is frowned upon in general is
that it undermines guarantees about the state of
the class with protected variables because subclasses
can mess up its intended behavior.

But there may be another way to do this. As Daniel
mentioned (in the office just now, not in e-mail), you
might be able to template out the reference to samples for:

void get_samples(size_t k,
size_t n,
std::vector<double>& samples)

It calls resize(), reserve() and insert() on the samples
object.

Another alternative to making _samples protected would be
to have a method return a const ref to it. (const is also
unsafe because it can be cast away, but as I said last time,
C(++) is just patently unsafe if clients are clever!)

- Bob
